readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module introduces Amazon EC2 as the core AWS compute service, from what an instance is and how multi-tenancy works to launching one from an AMI. It walks through the instance families, the three ways to call AWS APIs, and the EC2 pricing options with their discounts and trade-offs. It then shows how to keep applications available and efficient with Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, Elastic Load Balancing, and decoupled messaging through Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS and Amazon EventBridge.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 2 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Amazon EC2: what cloud compute is, EC2 versus on-premises servers, stopping versus terminating, multi-tenancy and how to launch, connect to and use an instance.

Compute in the Cloud

  1. Amazon EC2 Instance Types: the five instance families, how to tell them apart and how to pick a size.
  2. How to Provision AWS Resources: calling AWS APIs through the console, the AWS CLI and the AWS SDK, plus shared responsibility for EC2.
  3. Demo: Launching an Amazon EC2 Instance: the settings used to launch a web server and what an AMI does and does not do.
  4. Amazon EC2 Pricing: a side-by-side comparison of On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot Instances, Dedicated Hosts and Instances, and Capacity Reservations.

Auto Scaling and Load Balancing

  1. Scaling Amazon EC2: scalability versus elasticity, scaling up versus out, high availability and Auto Scaling groups.
  2. Directing Traffic with Elastic Load Balancing: how ELB spreads traffic, its routing methods and how it pairs with Auto Scaling.
  3. Messaging and Queuing: tight versus loose coupling, microservices, and the roles of Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS and Amazon EventBridge.

Module 2 Conclusion

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Amazon EC2 rents virtual servers on demand, faster, cheaper and more flexibly than owned hardware, and only running instances are billed.
  • Multi-tenancy lets isolated instances share a physical host, kept apart by a hypervisor that AWS manages.
  • Each instance family targets a bottleneck: balance (general purpose), CPU (compute optimized), memory (memory optimized), accelerators (accelerated computing) or local disk (storage optimized).
  • Every AWS action is an API call made through the console, the AWS CLI or the AWS SDK, and for unmanaged EC2 the customer handles the guest OS, updates and security groups.
  • An AMI is a configuration template rather than a backup, and launching from one AMI keeps instances identical.
  • On-Demand needs no commitment, Savings Plans (up to 72%) and Reserved Instances (up to 75%) reward 1- or 3-year commitments, and Spot Instances (up to 90%) suit interruptible work only.
  • Dedicated Hosts give a whole server with placement control, while Dedicated Instances give isolation from other accounts without a choice of server.
  • Scalability is long-term growth planning and elasticity is automatic real-time adjustment, which Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling delivers within an Auto Scaling group's minimum and maximum.
  • Elastic Load Balancing routes traffic across the instances Auto Scaling provides, and redundant instances across AZs give high availability.
  • Loose coupling isolates failures: Amazon SQS queues messages for later, Amazon SNS pushes them to subscribers at once, and Amazon EventBridge routes events between services.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

After this module you should be able to explain how Amazon EC2 and related cloud resources let applications grow with demand. You should also be able to compare instance types and pricing options and pick the right mix for a given business. Finally, you know which services manage traffic (Elastic Load Balancing and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling) and which manage communication between components (Amazon SQS and Amazon SNS).

introduction-to-amazon-ec2.html:
Introduction to Amazon EC2

Objectives

  • Explain how cloud is requested and managed.
  • Weigh virtual servers in the cloud against physical servers on premises.
  • Define for .

Notes

Compute in the cloud

  • Compute is processing power for applications, data and calculations, rented on demand as virtual machines with no hardware to own.
  • On AWS, the servers behind any business's (the coffee shop staff) are EC2 instances.

EC2 versus owning servers

  • Owning means upfront purchases, delivery waits, installation and fixed capacity.
  • AWS keeps huge capacity running, so instances are usable within minutes.
  • EC2 suits startups and enterprises and needs less setup and upkeep.
  • You pick server count, security, networking, storage and scale, which speeds up development and deployment.
  • Usage can swing widely, and you are never locked into servers you no longer need.

Stopping, terminating and billing

  • Only running instances are billed.
  • A stopped instance can be restarted later, a terminated one is deleted, and neither restarts by itself unless configured to.

Multi-tenancy

  • Many EC2 instances, which are virtual machines (VMs), share one physical host: multi-tenancy.
  • A on the host shares resources among them while isolating them, and AWS manages host, hypervisor and isolation.
  • The course also calls the sharers tenants, or users, kept apart for security and performance.

What you control

  • You choose the OS (Windows or Linux, across up to thousands of instances), fully control the software, and decide which requests get in and whether access is public or private.
  • Changing an instance's CPU and memory is .
  • What is new is not the VM but buying servers as a service: .

Launch, connect, use

  • Launch: pick an (CPU, memory, network performance) and an (OS plus optional software).
  • The AZ is usually set for you, bandwidth follows the instance type, and no backup plan or user count is needed.
  • Storage can be added after launch, though the demo sets a volume up front.
  • Connect: by network for applications, or SSH (Linux), Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) (Windows) or .
  • Use: run commands, install software, add storage, organize files.

Visuals

  • On-premises versus cloud timeline: slow, fixed hardware buying versus EC2's fast, pay-while-running model.
  • How Amazon EC2 works: launch, connect, use.

Key takeaways

  • EC2 is more flexible, cheaper and faster to start than owned servers, for any business size.
  • Billing stops when an instance stops, and only termination deletes it.
  • In multi-tenancy, isolated instances share a host whose hypervisor AWS manages.
  • A launch needs an instance type and an AMI, and instances resize vertically.

Scenarios

  • Servers for new websites: launch EC2 instances instead of buying hardware.

Terms

  • Compute: processing power for applications and calculations.
  • Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2): AWS's on-demand, resizable virtual server service.
  • EC2 instance: a virtual server on Amazon EC2.
  • Multi-tenancy: isolated VMs sharing one physical host.
  • Hypervisor: host software that shares resources among VMs and isolates them.
  • Vertical scaling: changing an instance's CPU and memory.
  • Compute as a Service: renting servers on demand.
  • Instance type: an instance's hardware profile of CPU, memory and network performance.
  • AWS Systems Manager: an AWS service for secure, simplified instance access.

amazon-ec2-instance-types.html:
Amazon EC2 Instance Types

Objectives

  • Tell the types apart by their strengths.
  • Match workloads to suitable types.

Notes

Instance families

  • Like coffee machines suited to different drinks, instance families each mix CPU, memory, storage and networking differently.
  • General purpose: balanced, for web services, code repositories and unpredictable workloads.
  • Compute optimized: CPU-heavy work like game servers, HPC, and scientific modeling.
  • Memory optimized: fast in-memory processing of large datasets, as in analytics and databases.
  • Accelerated computing: hardware accelerators such as GPUs, co-processors that do floating-point math, graphics, pattern matching and machine learning more efficiently than software running on a CPU.
  • Storage optimized: fast access to local data, as in data warehousing, large databases and I/O-heavy apps.
  • In analytics, real-time in-memory work points to memory optimized, while big local datasets needing low-latency access and steady, high disk throughput point to storage optimized.

Sizes

  • Bigger sizes cost more, so pick the smallest that performs well and switch later if needed.
  • Type names encode family and size.

Visuals

  • Instance types graphic: one marker per family.

Key takeaways

  • Unknown workload: start with general purpose.
  • Pick the family by the bottleneck: CPU, memory, accelerators or local disk.
  • Size trades performance for cost, and nothing is permanent.

Scenarios

  • A multiplayer game server: compute optimized.
  • A large in-memory database: memory optimized.
  • A on local disks: storage optimized.

Terms

  • Instance family: types sharing one resource mix.
  • General purpose instances: balanced, all-round instances.
  • Compute optimized instances: instances for CPU-heavy work.
  • Memory optimized instances: instances for big in-memory datasets.
  • Accelerated computing instances: instances with GPUs or other accelerators.
  • Storage optimized instances: instances for fast local storage.
  • Hardware accelerator: a co-processor that runs some functions more efficiently than CPU-run software.
  • Instance size: an instance's scale within its family.

how-to-provision-aws-resources.html:
How to Provision AWS Resources

Objectives

  • Choose between the console, the and the when working with AWS.
  • Split duties between customer and AWS.
  • Start telling managed from unmanaged services (EC2 is the unmanaged example, and managed services come later).

Notes

APIs behind every action

  • Every AWS task, from launching to stopping or changing an instance, is an request.
  • An application programming interface (API) gives fixed entry points to provision, configure and manage resources.
  • The console, the AWS CLI and the AWS SDK all call the same APIs.

AWS Management Console

  • A browser-based visual interface with search, quick service access and simplified workflows.
  • Best for learning, test environments, bills, monitoring, non-technical tasks and one-time manual setups.
  • Its mobile app checks resources, alarms and billing for several signed-in identities.
  • Repeating its screens for every production launch is slow and invites slips like a missed checkbox.

AWS CLI

  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) issues API calls as text commands on Windows, macOS or Linux, so repetitive work can be scripted, and automation keeps deployments predictable.
  • is an AWS-managed cloud terminal with the AWS CLI ready.
  • Demo: aws ec2 run-instances creates a new instance, and aws ec2 describe-availability-zones lists the Region's AZs.

AWS SDK

  • The AWS Software Development Kit (AWS SDK) lets code in languages like Python, C++, Java and .NET call AWS, with AWS docs and sample code.
  • The demo lists EC2 instances from a Python script.

Shared responsibility for compute

  • Under the , AWS covers hardware and infrastructure, and you cover what runs on it: applications, data and access.
  • EC2 is unmanaged, so you configure its security, the guest OS and its updates, and firewall rules called security groups.

Visuals

  • Interacting with AWS accordion: console, CLI and SDK, each with the user it suits.
  • Shared responsibility image: customer duties for an atop AWS infrastructure.

Key takeaways

  • All AWS interaction is API calls, made through one of three tools.
  • The console suits visual and one-off work, the CLI suits scripts, and the SDK suits application code.
  • With EC2, the customer owns the guest OS, updates and security groups.

Terms

  • API (application programming interface): a predefined way to manage resources programmatically.
  • AWS Management Console: AWS's web-based graphical interface.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI): a tool for calling AWS APIs with typed commands.
  • AWS Software Development Kit (AWS SDK): language libraries for calling AWS from code.
  • AWS CloudShell: a managed cloud terminal with the AWS CLI ready.
  • Unmanaged service: a service like EC2 where the customer handles security and management.
  • Security group: a customer-configured firewall for an EC2 instance.

Demo: Launching an Amazon EC2 Instance

Objectives

  • Identify the main settings for launching an .
  • Explain how AMIs keep scaled-out instances consistent.

Notes

Launching a web server

  • In the EC2 console's launch instance flow, the demo sets these.
  • Name: to find the instance later.
  • : OS and bundled apps, here the default Amazon Linux AMI.
  • : compute power, here t2.micro (1 vCPU, 1 GB memory, Free Tier).
  • : a public key on the instance and a private key you keep for logging in, created at launch or reused.
  • Network settings: allow HTTP from the internet.
  • Storage: an 8 GB gp3 volume.
  • : a launch script, here installing and starting Nginx, which the generic AMI lacks.
  • Browsing to the public IP address then shows the web page.

What an AMI is and is not

  • An AMI holds the OS, architecture, storage layout, preinstalled software and launch permissions.
  • It does not set size or networking, and it is no data store or backup, since instance data typically lives on volumes like Amazon EBS.
  • Build a custom AMI, use an AWS one for common operating systems and software, or buy one on .
  • Launching from one AMI with automated deployments gives identical setups, consistent dev and test, fewer errors, easier scaling and simpler large fleets.

Visuals

  • AMI timeline: contents, sources and repeatability of AMIs.

Key takeaways

  • Each setting has a job: AMI for software, instance type for hardware, storage for disk, key pair for login, network settings for traffic.
  • An AMI is a configuration template, not a backup.
  • User data configures an instance at launch.

Scenarios

  • A generic Linux instance must serve web pages: install Nginx with user data.
  • Identical servers for : launch them from one AMI.

Terms

  • Amazon Machine Image (AMI): a prebuilt image with an instance's OS, software and setup.
  • Key pair: public and private keys used to log in to an instance.
  • User data: a script run at launch to configure an instance.
  • Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS): volumes, such as gp3, that give an instance its disk.
  • AWS Marketplace: where third-party vendors sell specialized AMIs.

amazon-ec2-pricing.html:
Amazon EC2 Pricing

Objectives

  • Compare the ways to pay for .
  • Choose a pricing model to fit a workload.
  • Describe how Capacity Reservations work and how RI discounts flex.

Notes

Options at a glance

Option Commitment Max discount Best for
On-Demand None None New, unknown or test workloads
$/hour spend, 1 or 3 years 72% Steady, critical use, incl. Fargate, Lambda, SageMaker AI
1 or 3 years, one family and Region 75% Steady-state, predictable use
None, AWS can reclaim 90% Batch and other interruptible jobs
A whole physical server Pricier than RIs Compliance, security or licensing needs
Hardware only for your account Not stated Isolation without server control

Commitments and flexibility

  • On-Demand bills per hour or second, by and OS, and is where most customers learn their baseline usage.
  • Savings Plans and RIs both accept all upfront, partial upfront or no upfront payment.
  • A Savings Plan applies whatever the Region, tenancy, OS, family or size, while an RI stays within its family and Region.
  • Critical, always-on workloads that want dependable capacity and a predictable bill fit Savings Plans.
  • RI flexibility: the discount flows automatically to other sizes in the family, by , and across the Region's AZs, aiding distribution and .
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, What are Savings Plans? AWS Savings Plans give prices below On-Demand rates in exchange for committing to a set amount of compute usage per hour for one or three years.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, How Reserved Instance discounts are applied Reserved Instance flexibility means a regional Reserved Instance discount applies in any of its Region and, for most instance types, to any size in the same .

Spot, isolation and reservations

  • AWS warns two minutes before reclaiming a Spot Instance, so the job can save progress and resume later.
  • A Dedicated Host gives control over instance placement and resource allocation, which helps with compliance and with licensing such as Windows or Server.
  • Dedicated Instances are isolated from other accounts, though AWS picks the server, so they sit outside the multi-tenant model while keeping shared-infrastructure savings.
  • hold capacity in one AZ for critical workloads, billed at the On-Demand rate even when unused.
  • The course also says you pay only for the instances you run, without squaring this with the charge for unused reservations.

Visuals

  • Pricing flashcards: one card per model.
  • Dedicated Host versus Dedicated Instance graphic: a whole machine against a dedicated slice of one.
  • accordion: Savings Plans, Capacity Reservations and RI flexibility.

Key takeaways

  • Match the model to the usage: unknown means On-Demand, steady means Savings Plans or RIs, and interruptible but never critical means Spot.
  • Savings Plans flex across families, Regions and serverless services, and RIs do not.
  • Dedicated Hosts cost more than RIs, so use them only when you need server control.

Scenarios

  • Steady usage across EC2, Fargate and Lambda: one Savings Plan.
  • Isolation from other customers without choosing servers: Dedicated Instances.
  • A critical launch needing guaranteed capacity in one AZ: a Capacity Reservation.

Terms

  • On-Demand Instances: pay-while-running compute with no commitment.
  • Savings Plans: discounts for committing to steady hourly compute spend.
  • Reserved Instances (RIs): discounts for a 1- or 3-year term in one family and Region.
  • Spot Instances: discounted spare capacity that AWS can reclaim.
  • Dedicated Hosts: whole physical servers reserved for one customer.
  • Dedicated Instances: instances on hardware dedicated to one account.
  • Amazon EC2 Capacity Reservations: capacity held in one AZ at On-Demand rates.
  • Instance size footprint: the measure for applying an RI discount across sizes in a family.
  • AWS Fargate: a serverless compute option, see module 3.
  • AWS Lambda: a serverless compute option, see module 3.

scaling-amazon-ec2.html:
Scaling Amazon EC2

Objectives

  • Recognize and and how they differ on AWS.
  • Describe how AWS lets a business match compute capacity to shifting demand.

Notes

Why fixed capacity fails

  • A site that keeps timing out is usually getting more requests than it can serve.
  • Demand has busy and quiet seasons, and new businesses cannot predict peaks.
  • Buying for the peak wastes money and buying for the average leaves customers waiting, so capacity should track demand hour by hour.
  • The coffee stands for any instance output, like web responses.

Redundancy and high availability

  • One instance in a role is a single point of failure: lose the only order-taker and the business stops.
  • With a second, programmatically created copy, one keeps serving while a replacement for the failed one spins up.
  • Back-end instances need the same redundancy, for a highly available system.
  • Best practice is to spread redundant instances over multiple AZs in a Region, so the rest carry the load if one zone has trouble.

Scalability versus elasticity

  • Scalability looks ahead: long-term capacity planning so a system can absorb more users or work by adding resources.
  • Elasticity reacts in the moment: resources scale out automatically when demand spikes and back in when it falls, so each moment costs only what it needs.

Scaling out versus scaling up

  • (horizontal): more instances share the work in parallel.
  • (vertical): give running instances more power.
  • More power per instance does not always help, since a faster cashier cannot hurry an undecided customer, but extra cashiers serve more people at once.
  • Each tier scales on its own, so order-takers can outnumber drink-makers while the back end has no backlog, and nothing is overprovisioned.
  • After the rush, the surplus instances are scaled in.

Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

  • It adds instances as demand and key metrics rise and decommissions them as demand falls, keeping the desired number running every minute.
  • collects the performance, latency and other metrics that trigger these changes.
  • responds to demand in real time, and schedules capacity ahead of expected demand.
  • It improves availability, and you pay only for the EC2 instances it runs, while they run.

Auto Scaling groups

  • An is a set of EC2 instances that scales in and out within three settings.
  • Minimum capacity: the floor, launched as soon as the group is created (4 in the example).
  • Desired capacity: the count it aims to hold for the current load, defaulting to the minimum if unset (6).
  • Maximum capacity: the ceiling that prevents over-scaling and caps cost (12), with scaling between minimum and maximum.

Visuals

  • Scalability and elasticity timeline: an instance growing (up) beside instances multiplying (out), then capacity flexing with demand.
  • Auto Scaling group tabs: one group drawn at minimum (4), desired (6) and maximum (12) capacity.

Key takeaways

  • Scalability is planned, long-term growth, while elasticity is automatic, real-time adjustment.
  • Redundant instances across multiple AZs remove single points of failure.
  • Auto Scaling uses CloudWatch metrics to add and remove instances, dynamically or predictively.
  • An Auto Scaling group stays between its minimum and maximum and aims for its desired capacity.

Scenarios

  • A new store cannot predict its traffic spikes: let Auto Scaling follow demand.
  • An application runs in a single AZ: add redundant instances in another AZ.
  • More customers arrive, but a bigger server cannot serve any one faster: scale out.

Terms

  • Scalability: the ability to take on more load by adding resources, planned long term.
  • Elasticity: automatic, real-time growing and shrinking of resources with demand.
  • Scaling out (horizontal scaling): adding instances to work in parallel.
  • Scaling up (vertical scaling): making a running instance more powerful.
  • Scaling in: removing instances as demand falls.
  • High availability: staying in service with no single point of failure.
  • Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling: a service that adds and removes EC2 instances automatically with demand.
  • Dynamic scaling: Auto Scaling that reacts in real time.
  • Predictive scaling: Auto Scaling that schedules capacity ahead of anticipated demand.
  • Auto Scaling group: EC2 instances scaled together between set limits.
  • Amazon CloudWatch: the metrics service behind scaling decisions, see module 10.

directing-traffic-with-elastic-load-bala.html:
Directing Traffic with Elastic Load Balancing

Objectives

  • Explain why spreading traffic and scaling are hard on AWS.
  • Recognize what adds.
  • Describe how ELB and split the work.

Notes

Uneven load

  • Spreading a workload keeps any one resource from carrying it all, which boosts performance.
  • When customers crowd one cashier while others idle, a host at the door who sends each arrival to the shortest line fixes it.
  • On AWS a plays the host, so no sits idle or overloaded.

Load balancers and ELB

  • A load balancer receives incoming requests and decides which instance serves each one.
  • Third-party load balancers run on AWS, but you then own their upkeep: upgrades, patches, maintenance and failover.
  • Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) is AWS's managed option: set it up once and AWS does that upkeep.
  • "Elastic" means it grows and shrinks with traffic at no extra hourly cost.
  • It handles internal and external traffic and routes by , , or (see Terms).
  • In front of an it is the single entry point, spreading requests evenly over whatever instances exist.

Decoupling tiers

  • An ordering website has tiers such as ordering, production and storage.
  • Without ELB, every front-end instance must track every back-end instance, which is unmanageable at hundreds or thousands.
  • ELB is Regional, so front ends need only its single URL, and it passes each request to the back-end instance with the fewest outstanding requests.
  • A new back-end instance just tells ELB it is ready, unseen by the front end, so each scales on its own and the architecture is decoupled.

ELB and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

  • They are separate services with complementary jobs: Auto Scaling sets how many instances run, and ELB spreads traffic across them.
  • ELB never adds, removes or resizes instances itself.
  • Together they keep performance consistent and availability high.

Example: a hospital patient portal

  • Quiet start: a few early patients, and existing servers cope.
  • (the course's tab says ""): at peaks like early mornings or before weekends, servers are added automatically, which lesson 6 calls horizontal scaling.
  • Load balancing: new requests go to a less busy server, so none is overwhelmed.
  • ELB plus Auto Scaling keeps the portal reliable at peak demand.

Visuals

  • ELB benefits flashcards: traffic distribution, automatic scaling and simplified management.
  • Routing methods graphic: one column per routing method.
  • Patient portal tabs: quiet, scaled out, then balanced.

Key takeaways

  • ELB benefits: even traffic spread, automatic scaling as instances come and go, and less management thanks to decoupled tiers and AWS-run maintenance and failover.
  • Auto Scaling changes the instance count, and ELB only routes traffic across those instances.
  • ELB is a Regional single entry point that scales without raising hourly cost.

Scenarios

  • Front-end instances struggle to track changing back-end instances: put ELB between the tiers.

Terms

  • Load balancer: a component that distributes incoming requests across instances.
  • Elastic Load Balancing (ELB): AWS's managed, Regional service that spreads traffic across EC2 instances and other resources.
  • Round Robin: routing that cycles through servers in order.
  • Least Connections: routing toward the server with the fewest open connections.
  • IP Hash: routing that pins each client IP address to one server.
  • Least Response Time: routing toward the fastest-responding server to cut latency.
  • Tier: one functional layer of an application, such as ordering or storage.

messaging-and-queuing.html:
Messaging and Queuing

Objectives

  • Show how buffers messages between components.
  • Explain how sends messages out through publish-subscribe.
  • Distinguish tight from loose coupling.
  • Explain why a queue between components makes their communication sturdier.

Notes

Why direct handoffs break

  • A cashier handing paper orders straight to a barista works only while both are free at the same moment.
  • If the barista is busy or on break, the cashier is stuck and orders slow down or get dropped.
  • Posting orders to an order board removes that dependency, and buffering messages this way is called .

Tight versus loose coupling

  • Tightly coupled: components talk directly, so a failure or change in one hurts the others or the whole system, as when Application B goes down and Application A starts failing.
  • Loosely coupled: a message queue sits between them, so A keeps sending while B is down and messages wait until B handles them.
  • Loose coupling contains failures instead of letting them cascade, and it is the target for AWS architectures.

From monoliths to microservices

  • Reliability and resilience come from a service-oriented design.
  • A traditional monolith tightly couples its database logic, web servers, user interface and business logic, so one failure can take down the whole application.
  • Microservices loosely couple those parts, so the rest keep working and talking when one fails, adding availability, resilience and flexibility.

Amazon EventBridge

  • EventBridge, SNS and SQS all support scalable event-driven or message-based communication between application parts.
  • EventBridge is serverless: custom apps, AWS services or third-party software feed it events, and it forwards them to the applications that need them.
  • It handles the event pipeline end to end: intake, filtering, transformation and delivery.
  • Food delivery example: one meal order must trigger payment, a restaurant alert, an inventory check and driver dispatch at once.
  • EventBridge routes events like "order placed" to each service, copes with peaks, keeps services independent and holds events for a service that is down until it recovers.

Amazon SQS

  • SQS is a message queue: producers drop messages in, and a consumer later picks each one up, processes it and deletes it.
  • It moves any volume of messages between components without losing them, and the receiver need not be available at send time.
  • In the coffee shop, the order board is the queue and each order is a message whose contents (name, drink, time) are the .
  • Queues need little setup and grow automatically while staying reliable.
  • Customer support example: instead of waiting on a busy specialist, the agent adds tickets to an SQS queue and the specialist works through the backlog.

Amazon SNS

  • SNS is publish-subscribe: publishers send a message to a topic, and subscribers such as web servers, email addresses and Lambda functions receive it.
  • Unlike SQS, SNS does not park messages for later, so in the coffee shop it is the barista calling out a finished drink, not the order board.
  • It can also reach people directly, fanning out by text message, email or mobile push, for example to say an order is ready.
  • Product updates example: one email on every topic left customers unhappy and disengaged, so the company split updates into topics for new products, offers and events, and customers subscribe only to what they want.

Visuals

  • Decoupling timeline: a fragile monolith, then resilient microservices.
  • EventBridge food delivery graphic: the four services one order triggers.
  • SQS customer support tabs: scenario, challenge and queue-based fix.
  • SNS product updates graphic: topics, subscriptions, then tailored notifications.

Key takeaways

  • Tight coupling lets one failure spread, while loose coupling keeps components independent.
  • Amazon SQS holds messages until a consumer is ready, so senders never wait on receivers.
  • Amazon SNS pushes each message to topic subscribers immediately, including people by push, SMS and email.
  • routes events to many services and holds them for a service that is down.
  • Use SQS when work can be processed later and SNS when recipients must hear at once.

Scenarios

  • Work arrives while the processing service is busy or offline: queue it in Amazon SQS.
  • Customers want only some kinds of updates: separate Amazon SNS topics.

Terms

  • Messaging and queuing: passing messages between applications through a buffer.
  • Tightly coupled architecture: components that depend directly on each other, so one failure spreads.
  • Loosely coupled architecture: independent components, so one failure stays contained.
  • Monolithic application: an application whose components are tightly coupled.
  • Microservices architecture: an application design with loosely coupled components.
  • Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS): a queue service that reliably holds messages between components.
  • Payload: the data inside a message.
  • Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS): a publish-subscribe service that pushes messages to topic subscribers.
  • SNS topic: the channel publishers send to and subscribers sign up for.
  • Fan out: pushing one notification to many end users via mobile push, SMS or email.
  • Amazon EventBridge: a serverless event router between applications and services.
