questions.takeaway: When more users arrive but a bigger server would not speed each request, scale out by adding instances.

read.text: More power per instance does not always help, since a faster cashier cannot hurry an undecided customer, but extra cashiers serve more people at once.

questions.stem: Weekend crowds are flooding the cafe's ordering site. Each order is quick to handle, so a more powerful server would gain little time per order. Which approach lets the site serve more customers at the same time?

options.why: More power per instance does not help here, since each order is already handled quickly.
Adding instances that work in parallel serves more customers at once, like extra cashiers.
Scaling in removes instances, which would make the weekend crowd wait longer.
Redundancy across zones protects against failure but is not the answer to more customers.

questions.takeaway: Elasticity works in both directions, scaling back in automatically once a rush is over.

read.text: Elasticity reacts in the moment: resources scale out automatically when demand spikes and back in when it falls, so each moment costs only what it needs.

questions.stem: After a festival weekend, the cafe's ordering site keeps running every extra instance it added, though orders are back to normal. Which cloud benefit would have removed those instances automatically as orders fell?

options.why: Agility is about trying and changing things quickly, not shrinking capacity as demand drops.
Scalability plans long-term growth, and it does not shed instances when a busy weekend ends.
Elastic resources scale back in automatically as demand falls, so the quiet days stop costing extra.
High availability keeps the site up through failures, and it does not trim instances after a rush.

questions.takeaway: Load balancing improves performance by keeping any one resource from carrying the whole workload.

read.text: Spreading a workload keeps any one resource from carrying it all, which boosts performance.

questions.stem: Why does spreading incoming requests over several servers improve performance?

options.text: The hourly cost stays flat as traffic grows
options.why: ELB grows with traffic at no extra hourly cost, but that is a cost benefit, not why spreading speeds things up.

options.text: Front ends need only one address to call
options.why: A single entry point simplifies the front end, but it does not explain why spreading requests helps performance.

options.text: No single resource has to do all the work
options.why: When the work is shared, no single resource is overloaded, so performance holds up.

options.text: AWS handles the patching and the failover
options.why: AWS-run upkeep lightens management, but it does not explain why spreading requests helps performance.

questions.takeaway: ELB is the managed load balancer, so AWS does the patching, upgrades and failover that a self-run one needs.

read.text: Third-party load balancers run on AWS, but you then own their upkeep: upgrades, patches, maintenance and failover.

questions.stem: The cafe runs third-party software on its own EC2 instance to hand each incoming order to one of its servers. It is tired of patching, upgrading and handling failover for that software. Which AWS service does the same job while AWS takes over the upkeep?

options.why: Auto Scaling adjusts the number of instances but does not route requests between them.
CloudFront caches content close to viewers and is not a managed replacement for a load balancer in front of instances.
Global Accelerator speeds up the network path to an application rather than replacing the cafe's load balancer.
ELB is the managed load balancer, so AWS handles its patches, upgrades and failover once it is set up.

questions.takeaway: Auto Scaling adds the instances, and ELB, as the single entry point, spreads traffic onto them.

read.text: In front of an Auto Scaling group it is the single entry point, spreading requests evenly over whatever instances exist.

questions.stem: During the Saturday rush, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling adds servers to the cafe's menu site fleet, which sits behind ELB. Which fact explains how the new servers start getting customer requests?

options.text: Auto Scaling sets how many instances are running
options.why: This is true, but setting the count only adds the servers and sends them no requests.

options.text: ELB routes requests across all running instances
options.why: ELB is the single entry point and spreads requests over whatever instances Auto Scaling has running.

options.text: ELB is a Regional service that AWS manages
options.why: Being Regional and managed is true of ELB but does not explain how new servers get traffic.

options.text: ELB grows with traffic at no added hourly cost
options.why: ELB's own elasticity is true, yet it says nothing about requests reaching the new servers.

questions.takeaway: Auto Scaling changes how many instances run, and ELB only spreads traffic across them.

read.text: Auto Scaling changes the instance count, and ELB only routes traffic across those instances.

questions.stem: The cafe pairs Elastic Load Balancing with Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling. Which jobs belong to Auto Scaling rather than to ELB? (Select TWO.)

options.why: Adding instances as demand rises is Auto Scaling's job, since ELB never adds instances itself.
Spreading requests is ELB's job, routing traffic over whatever instances Auto Scaling keeps running.
Neither service resizes instances, since ELB never does and Auto Scaling changes the count rather than the size.

options.text: Giving front ends one address to call
options.why: ELB is the single Regional entry point, so giving front ends one address is its job, not Auto Scaling's.
Auto Scaling sets how many instances run, while ELB only routes traffic across them.
Gathering performance and latency metrics is the job of Amazon CloudWatch, and Auto Scaling only acts on them.

questions.takeaway: ELB can route in turn, by fewest connections, by client IP or by fastest response.

read.text: Round Robin: routing that cycles through servers in order.

questions.stem: Match each ELB routing method to how it chooses a server.

pairs.right: Works through the servers in a fixed rotation
pairs.why: Round Robin cycles through the servers in a fixed order.

pairs.right: Picks the server holding the fewest live sessions
pairs.why: Least Connections sends the request to the least busy server by open connections.

pairs.right: Sends a given client to one server every time
pairs.why: IP Hash ties a client IP address to one server so its requests land there each time.

pairs.right: Picks the server with the lowest latency now
pairs.why: Least Response Time favors the quickest server to cut latency.

questions.takeaway: In an ELB plus Auto Scaling setup, Auto Scaling sets the instance count and ELB only routes traffic.

read.text: They are separate services with complementary jobs: Auto Scaling sets how many instances run, and ELB spreads traffic across them.

questions.stem: The cafe's menu site runs on a fleet of servers behind ELB and gets a rush every Saturday morning. Which service decides how many servers are running during the rush?

options.why: Auto Scaling sets the instance count, adding instances for the rush and removing them afterward.
ELB only spreads traffic across the instances that exist and never adds or removes any.
Compute Optimizer recommends better instance sizes but does not add or remove instances for the rush.
Lambda runs code in response to events and does not manage how many EC2 instances run.

questions.takeaway: A load balancer receives each request and chooses the instance that serves it.

read.text: A load balancer receives incoming requests and decides which instance serves each one.

questions.stem: What does a load balancer do with each incoming request?

options.text: Adds a new instance to handle it
options.why: Adding instances changes the fleet size, which a load balancer does not do.

options.text: Holds it until a consumer reads it
options.why: Holding work until a consumer is ready describes a message queue, not a load balancer.

options.text: Copies it to every running instance
options.why: A load balancer sends each request to one instance rather than to all of them.

options.text: Picks which instance will serve it
options.why: A load balancer takes in each request and decides which instance should serve it.

questions.takeaway: When some instances are overloaded and others idle, a load balancer in front spreads requests across them.

read.text: A load balancer receives incoming requests and decides which instance serves each one.

questions.stem: The cafe's ordering site runs on several EC2 instances. During the lunch rush one instance is swamped while the others barely work. What should sit in front of the instances so the requests are shared out?

options.why: An Auto Scaling group changes how many instances run, but it does not choose which one gets each request.
A load balancer takes each incoming request and picks an instance for it, so no instance is swamped while others idle.
An AMI is a template for launching instances and plays no part in sending requests to them.
An Availability Zone is a place where instances run, not a component that splits traffic between them.

questions.takeaway: To keep each client on the same server by IP address, route with IP Hash.

read.text: IP Hash: routing that pins each client IP address to one server.

questions.stem: The cafe's loyalty app keeps each customer's session on one server, so a returning customer's device must keep landing on that same server. Which routing method should the load balancer use?

options.why: Round Robin moves through the servers in turn, so a customer's requests would land on different servers.
Least Connections picks whichever server is least busy, which can change from one request to the next.
IP Hash ties each client IP address to one server, so a customer keeps reaching the same one.
Least Response Time picks the quickest server at that moment, not the same server each time.

questions.takeaway: ELB decouples tiers because front ends call one Regional address and new back ends register with ELB, not with the front end.

read.text: ELB is Regional, so front ends need only its single URL, and it passes each request to the back-end instance with the fewest outstanding requests.

questions.stem: The cafe's ordering front end keeps losing track of its back-end servers as they come and go. The cafe puts ELB between the two tiers. Which traits of ELB fix this problem? (Select TWO.)

options.text: AWS handles its patches and failover
options.why: This is true of ELB, but it removes upkeep work and does not stop the front end from tracking back ends.

options.text: Front ends reach it at one Regional address
options.why: With one Regional address to call, the front end no longer needs a list of back-end servers.

options.text: It adds back-end servers as demand rises
options.why: ELB never adds or removes instances, since setting the instance count is the job of Auto Scaling.

options.text: It handles internal and external traffic
options.why: This is true of ELB, but the kind of traffic it takes does nothing for the front end's tracking problem.

options.text: New back ends tell it when they are ready
options.why: A new back end signs in with ELB, unseen by the front end, so the front end never has to learn about it.

questions.takeaway: EventBridge, SNS and SQS are the AWS services for event-driven and message-based communication between components.

read.text: EventBridge, SNS and SQS all support scalable event-driven or message-based communication between application parts.

questions.stem: Which AWS services support scalable event-driven or message-based communication between the parts of an application? (Select THREE.)

options.why: EventBridge routes events between application parts, so it supports event-driven communication.
SQS passes messages between components through a queue, so it supports message-based communication.
SNS pushes messages from publishers to subscribers, so it supports message-based communication.
API Gateway builds and manages APIs that clients call, and it does not carry events or messages between application parts.
Lambda runs code when an event arrives, but it does not route or hold events and messages between application parts.
SES sends bulk email from apps to people, and it does not carry events or messages between application parts.

questions.takeaway: Messaging and queuing puts a buffer such as an SQS queue between sender and receiver, so the sender never waits on the receiver.

read.text: If the barista is busy or on break, the cashier is stuck and orders slow down or get dropped.

questions.stem: The cafe's ordering app hands each order straight to its kitchen app, and orders get dropped whenever the kitchen app is busy or offline. Which service lets the ordering app keep sending orders while the kitchen app is unavailable?

options.why: An SQS queue holds each order until the kitchen app picks it up, so the ordering app never waits for it.
SNS pushes messages to subscribers but does not park them for later, so an offline kitchen app misses them.
ELB spreads requests over running instances, and it has nowhere to hold orders while the kitchen app is down.
Auto Scaling changes how many instances run, but it does not hold orders while the kitchen app is unavailable.

questions.takeaway: When work arrives faster than a receiver can handle it, or while it is offline, queue it in Amazon SQS.

read.text: It moves any volume of messages between components without losing them, and the receiver need not be available at send time.

questions.stem: The cafe's catering app logs large orders faster than the kitchen planner can review them, and the planner is sometimes offline. Which service lets the orders wait until the planner is ready to work through them?

options.why: SQS keeps each order in a queue until the planner is ready, even when the planner is offline at send time.
SNS pushes messages to subscribers right away and does not keep them for a planner who is offline.
ELB spreads incoming requests across running targets, and it does not hold orders for a planner who is offline.
API Gateway builds and manages APIs, and it does not buffer orders until a busy receiver is free.

questions.takeaway: Messaging and queuing passes messages between applications through a buffer instead of a direct handoff.

read.text: Messaging and queuing: passing messages between applications through a buffer.

questions.stem: Which description matches the idea of messaging and queuing?

options.text: Applications pass data through a holding area read later
options.why: Messaging and queuing puts a buffer between applications, so data waits there until the receiver handles it.

options.text: Applications pass data through direct calls that wait
options.why: Direct calls that wait for a reply are a tightly coupled handoff, not a buffer between applications.

options.text: Applications pass requests through a balancer to servers
options.why: Spreading requests across servers is load balancing, which does not hold data for a receiver to read later.

options.text: Applications pass data through copies in a second Region
options.why: Copying data to another Region protects against outages but does not buffer data between applications.

questions.takeaway: Loosely coupled components fail independently and keep sending while a receiver is unavailable.

read.text: Loosely coupled: a message queue sits between them, so A keeps sending while B is down and messages wait until B handles them.

questions.stem: The cafe's ordering app sends every order to its kitchen app through a message queue, and during the lunch rush the kitchen app crashes. Which things happen before the kitchen app comes back? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The ordering app keeps taking new orders
options.why: The queue accepts each order, so the ordering app keeps working instead of failing along with the kitchen app.

options.text: The kitchen app works through the backlog
options.why: Working through the waiting orders needs a running kitchen app, so it only starts once the app is back.

options.text: New orders wait in the queue for the kitchen
options.why: Each order the ordering app sends stays in the queue until the kitchen app is back to handle it.

options.text: The ordering app retries until the kitchen replies
options.why: The ordering app hands each order to the queue and moves on, so it never waits on a reply from the kitchen app.

options.text: The kitchen app takes the next order off the queue
options.why: A crashed kitchen app takes nothing off the queue, so every order stays there until the app is back.

questions.takeaway: A queue between components loosely couples them, so one component failing does not drag the other down.

read.text: Tightly coupled: components talk directly, so a failure or change in one hurts the others or the whole system, as when Application B goes down and Application A starts failing.

questions.stem: The cafe's ordering app calls its receipt app directly, and whenever the receipt app crashes the ordering app starts failing too. Which design change keeps the ordering app working while the receipt app is down?

options.text: Put a message queue between the two apps
options.why: With a queue in between, the ordering app keeps sending and the messages wait until the receipt app recovers.

options.text: Run the ordering app in two Availability Zones
options.why: Two Availability Zones protect the ordering app from a data center outage, but it still calls the crashed receipt app directly.

options.text: Scale the ordering app with EC2 Auto Scaling
options.why: Auto Scaling adds ordering capacity as demand rises, but every new instance still fails when the receipt app is down.

options.text: Take regular backups of the receipt app data
options.why: Backups let the receipt app's data be restored later, but they do not stop the direct calls from failing now.

questions.takeaway: In SQS, producers add messages and a consumer later picks each one up, processes it and deletes it.

read.text: SQS is a message queue: producers drop messages in, and a consumer later picks each one up, processes it and deletes it.

questions.stem: In Amazon SQS, which step comes right after a consumer finishes processing a message?

options.text: The consumer deletes it from the queue
options.why: An SQS consumer picks up a message, processes it and then deletes it from the queue.

options.text: The consumer picks it up from the queue
options.why: Picking the message up is a real SQS step, but it comes before processing, not after.

options.text: The consumer reads the payload inside it
options.why: Reading the payload is part of processing the message, so it happens before the step the stem asks about.

options.text: The producer drops it into the queue
options.why: The producer adds the message at the very start, long before any consumer processes it.

questions.takeaway: In publish-subscribe, publishers send to a topic and every subscriber of that topic receives the message.

read.text: SNS is publish-subscribe: publishers send a message to a topic, and subscribers such as web servers, email addresses and Lambda functions receive it.

questions.stem: Match each publish-subscribe role to what it does.

pairs.right: Sends a message to a topic
pairs.why: A publisher sends its message to a topic rather than to each recipient one by one.

pairs.right: The channel that recipients sign up for
pairs.why: A topic is the channel publishers send to and subscribers sign up for.

pairs.right: Receives each message sent to its topic
pairs.why: A subscriber, such as an email address or a Lambda function, gets every message published to its topic.

questions.takeaway: In an event-driven design, one event such as an order can trigger several independent services at once.

read.text: Food delivery example: one meal order must trigger payment, a restaurant alert, an inventory check and driver dispatch at once.

questions.stem: When a customer places an order in the cafe's delivery app, payment, a kitchen alert, a stock check and driver dispatch must all start at once. Which design fits this setup?

options.text: Each service reacts on its own to an order-placed event
options.why: Each service reacts independently to the same order event, so all four start at once, which is an event-driven design.

options.text: Each service polls one shared queue and takes orders in turn
options.why: A queue hands each order to a single consumer, so only one of the four services would get each order.

options.text: The ordering service calls each of the other services in sequence
options.why: Direct calls in sequence tightly couple the services and start them one after another, not all at once.

options.text: A load balancer sends each order to one of the four services
options.why: A load balancer picks one target per request, so one order would start only one of the four services.

questions.takeaway: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event router that connects applications and services.

read.text: Amazon EventBridge: a serverless event router between applications and services.

questions.stem: Which statement describes Amazon EventBridge?

options.text: A serverless router linking applications and services
options.why: EventBridge is a serverless router that forwards what happens in one application to the services that need it.

options.text: A queue that keeps each message until one consumer takes it
options.why: Keeping messages for a single consumer to pick up later describes Amazon SQS, not EventBridge.

options.text: A service that sends marketing and receipt email to customers
options.why: Sending email from applications is the job of Amazon SES, not a serverless router.

options.text: A service that collects streaming data for real-time analysis
options.why: Collecting streaming data for analysis describes Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, not EventBridge.

questions.takeaway: In publish-subscribe, one message sent to a topic goes straight to every subscriber.

read.text: SNS is publish-subscribe: publishers send a message to a topic, and subscribers such as web servers, email addresses and Lambda functions receive it.

questions.stem: The cafe publishes one "drink ready" message to an SNS topic that has a web server, a staff email address and a Lambda function subscribed. Which statement describes what happens to that message?

options.text: Subscribers choose which topics they join
options.why: This is true of SNS, but all three already subscribe, so it does not say what happens to the message.

options.text: A queue would hold it until a consumer polls
options.why: That describes SQS, while this message goes to an SNS topic that parks nothing for later.

options.text: Every subscriber gets it at the same time
options.why: In publish-subscribe, a message sent to a topic is pushed at once to all of its subscribers.

options.text: SNS can also notify people by text message
options.why: Text messages are a true SNS option, but none of these three subscribers is a phone number.

questions.takeaway: SNS pushes a message to every listener at once instead of parking it in a queue for later.

read.text: Unlike SQS, SNS does not park messages for later, so in the coffee shop it is the barista calling out a finished drink, not the order board.

questions.stem: In the cafe, which everyday action works most like Amazon SNS?

options.text: The barista announcing that a drink is ready
options.why: An announcement reaches everyone listening at once and is not kept for later, just like an SNS message.

options.text: Orders pinned to a board until someone is free
options.why: A board that keeps orders until someone is free works like an SQS queue, which SNS is not.

options.text: The cashier writing a name on each paper cup
options.why: Writing details on a cup is like the payload of a message, not the way SNS delivers it.

options.text: The register adding up the total for each bill
options.why: Totaling a bill is processing work, not pushing a message out to many listeners.

questions.takeaway: When events from many sources need filtering, transforming and routing to several services, choose EventBridge.

read.text: EventBridge is serverless: custom apps, AWS services or third-party software feed it events, and it forwards them to the applications that need them.

questions.stem: The cafe's app, several AWS services and a third-party payment tool each send a notice whenever something happens, such as a new order. Each notice must be filtered and reshaped, then forwarded to only the services that need it. Which service fits?

options.why: EventBridge takes in notices from custom apps, AWS services and third-party tools, then filters, transforms and delivers them.
SQS holds messages for a consumer to pick up later, but it does not filter, reshape and route them to many services.
SNS pushes each message to its topic subscribers, but it does not reshape the messages from third-party tools first.
Kinesis Data Streams ingests streaming data for apps to read, not filtering, reshaping and routing notices between services.

questions.takeaway: When people must hear right away by text, email or push, use SNS; SQS is for work that can wait.

read.text: Amazon SNS pushes each message to topic subscribers immediately, including people by push, SMS and email.

questions.stem: The cafe wants to text and email each customer the moment their drink is ready, with nothing held back for later. Which service fits?

options.why: SNS pushes each message to subscribers at once and can reach people by text message and email.
SQS holds messages until a consumer is ready, so it suits deferred work rather than instant alerts to people.
EventBridge routes events between applications and services, and it does not text or email customers directly.
Kinesis Data Streams collects streaming data for processing and does not notify people by text or email.

questions.takeaway: AWS architectures aim for loose coupling so a failure in one component stays contained.

read.text: Loose coupling contains failures instead of letting them cascade, and it is the target for AWS architectures.

questions.stem: Which design approach does AWS aim for so that a failure in one component stays contained?

options.why: Tightly coupled components depend on each other directly, so one failure spreads to the rest.
Vertical scaling changes one instance's CPU and memory, which does not stop failures spreading.
Loose coupling keeps components independent, so a failure stays contained, and it is the AWS target.
Multi-tenancy is about instances sharing one physical host, not about how components depend on each other.

questions.takeaway: An application whose parts are all tightly coupled is a monolith, so one failure can stop the whole thing.

read.text: A traditional monolith tightly couples its database logic, web servers, user interface and business logic, so one failure can take down the whole application.

questions.stem: Which term names an application whose database logic, web servers, user interface and business logic are all tightly coupled?

options.why: A monolith binds all of those parts tightly together, so one failure can take down the whole application.
Microservices loosely couple those parts, the opposite of the tight binding the stem describes.
An event-driven design has independent services react to events instead of binding the parts tightly.
Publish-subscribe sends messages to topic subscribers and does not describe parts bound into one application.

questions.takeaway: Separate publish-subscribe topics let each subscriber receive only the kinds of messages they signed up for.

read.text: Product updates example: one email on every topic left customers unhappy and disengaged, so the company split updates into topics for new products, offers and events, and customers subscribe only to what they want.

questions.stem: The cafe emails one newsletter covering every subject to all customers, and many of them stop reading it. Which change lets customers pick the subjects they receive?

options.text: Publish each kind of update to its own SNS topic
options.why: With one topic per kind of update, each customer subscribes only to the topics they want.

options.text: Publish every update to one shared SNS topic
options.why: One shared topic still sends every update to every subscriber, so customers cannot pick what they get.

options.text: Hold every update in an SQS queue before sending
options.why: A queue only delays the updates for later processing, and every customer still gets every subject.

options.text: Send every update as bulk email with Amazon SES
options.why: SES delivers bulk email reliably, but every customer still receives the same newsletter on every subject.

questions.takeaway: Breaking a monolith into loosely coupled microservices lets the rest of an application run when one part fails.

read.text: A traditional monolith tightly couples its database logic, web servers, user interface and business logic, so one failure can take down the whole application.

questions.stem: The cafe's website bundles its menu pages, payment logic and database code into one application, and a payment bug takes the whole site offline. Which design would keep the menu pages up when payments fail?

options.text: Split its parts into separate microservices
options.why: Microservices keep the menu pages separate from payments, so they keep running when payments fail.

options.text: Run several copies of it behind a load balancer
options.why: Every copy carries the same payment bug, so the load balancer has no healthy copy left to send visitors to.

options.text: Place it in an Auto Scaling group across two zones
options.why: Auto Scaling adds more copies of the same coupled application, and each one fails on the payment bug.

options.text: Keep a standby copy of it ready in a second Region
options.why: The standby copy holds the same payment bug, so switching to it still takes the whole site down.

labs.title: Launch the order server
labs.brief: The cafe's online ordering site needs one EC2 instance that takes orders day and night, all year, and an order lost to a stopped server is a lost sale. The site uses CPU, memory and network about evenly, the owner wants a discount for use she can predict all year, and staff update the site by logging in over SSH from the cafe's own network. Pick the instance family and how to pay for it, then set which traffic the security group lets in.

options.label: General purpose
options.detail: A balanced mix of CPU, memory, storage and networking.

options.label: Compute optimized
options.detail: Built for CPU-heavy work such as game servers and scientific modeling.

options.label: Memory optimized
options.detail: Built for fast in-memory processing of large datasets.

options.label: Accelerated computing
options.detail: Adds hardware accelerators such as GPUs.

options.label: Storage optimized
options.detail: Built for fast access to large data on local disks.

options.label: On-Demand Instances
options.detail: No commitment, billed per hour or second while it runs.

options.label: Savings Plans
options.detail: Commit to an hourly compute spend for 1 or 3 years.

options.label: Reserved Instances
options.detail: Commit for 1 or 3 years to one family and Region.

options.label: Spot Instances
options.detail: Spare capacity that AWS can reclaim after a two-minute warning.

options.label: Dedicated Hosts
options.detail: A whole physical server for the cafe alone.

options.label: Dedicated Instances
options.detail: Hardware used only by the cafe's account, on a server AWS picks.

fields.label: Allow SSH in from the cafe's network only

goals.label: The family fits a balanced web order server
goals.hint: A web server that leans on no single resource wants a family that mixes CPU, memory and networking evenly.

goals.label: The purchase option earns a commitment discount for steady, uninterrupted use
goals.hint: Ask whether a steady, predictable workload that must never be interrupted earns a discount in return for a 1 or 3 year commitment.

goals.label: Customers reach the site over HTTPS and only the cafe can log in
goals.hint: A security group blocks every inbound sender until a rule allows it, so open only what each kind of visitor needs.

notes.title: Demo: Launching an Amazon EC2 Instance
Subnets, Security Groups, and Network Access Control Lists

lines: General purpose instances mix CPU, memory and networking evenly, so they suit a web server that leans on no single resource.
A server that runs steadily all year earns a Savings Plan or Reserved Instance discount, while Spot fits only work that can be interrupted.
A security group lets in only the traffic its rules allow, so customers get HTTPS and only the cafe gets SSH.

questions.takeaway: When a workload's needs are still unknown, start on general purpose instances and adjust later.

read.text: Unknown workload: start with general purpose.

questions.stem: The cafe is launching a new ordering website and has no idea yet whether it will lean on CPU, memory or disk. Which EC2 instance family is the sensible starting point?

options.why: This family pays off only when CPU is the known bottleneck, which the cafe cannot say yet.
Its balanced mix suits a workload whose needs are still unknown, so it is the safe place to start.
This family targets big in-memory datasets, a need the new website has not shown.
This family serves heavy local disk access, which nothing in this scenario calls for.

questions.takeaway: Interruptible, non-critical batch work fits Spot Instances and their deep discount on spare capacity.

read.text: Match the model to the usage: unknown means On-Demand, steady means Savings Plans or RIs, and interruptible but never critical means Spot.

questions.stem: Each night the cafe runs a batch job that resizes menu photos. The job can stop at any point and pick up later, and nothing depends on when it finishes. Which pricing option costs the least for this job?

options.why: Dedicated hardware adds isolation the photo job does not need and gives no deep discount.
On-Demand works but charges full price for a job that could run on cheaper spare capacity.
Spot gives the deepest discount, and an interruption only pauses a job that can resume later.
A reservation suits steady, always-on use, not a short nightly job that can be interrupted.

questions.takeaway: When instances in one subnet need different port rules, use security groups, which work per instance.

read.text: Instances in one subnet may need different rules about who may contact them and on which ports, which calls for instance-level control.

questions.stem: The cafe's web server and its reporting server sit in the same subnet. The web server should accept only HTTPS, while the reporting server needs a different port open. Which control lets the cafe set these rules separately for each server?

options.why: A network ACL applies to the whole subnet, so it cannot give two instances in it different rules.
A security group filters traffic for one instance, so each server can have its own port rules.
An internet gateway links the VPC to the internet and holds no per-server port rules.
A NAT gateway lets private instances start outside connections and does not set port rules per server.

labs.title: Morning rush
labs.brief: The cafe's ordering site is quiet at night, then orders climb fast toward a breakfast peak and taper off by evening, and the breakfast climb starts at the same hour every morning. Set the Auto Scaling group's limits, how it scales and whether a load balancer spreads the orders, so almost no order drops and the day stays within 120 lab credits. The hourly orders, the 50 orders one instance takes an hour and its price of 2 lab credits an hour are all lab values.

params.label: Put a load balancer in front of the group

goals.label: At most 1% of the day's orders are dropped
goals.hint: Capacity must already be there when the breakfast climb starts, reach the peak, and be shared, since a group with no single entry point leaves one instance taking every order.

goals.label: The day costs at most 120 lab credits
goals.hint: Every running instance is billed each hour whether busy or idle, so capacity sized for the peak should scale back in once the rush is over.

goals.label: At least one instance is ready every hour of the day
goals.hint: The minimum is the floor the group never drops below, however quiet the hour, so the site always has something serving it.

notes.title: Directing Traffic with Elastic Load Balancing

lines: Predictive scaling adds instances ahead of a rush the cafe expects, while dynamic scaling reacts after demand has already climbed.
The group never runs fewer instances than its minimum or more than its maximum, so the maximum must reach the breakfast peak and the minimum keeps the site up overnight.
Auto Scaling sets how many instances run, and the load balancer spreads orders across them; scaling out without it still overloads one instance.
Scaling in once the rush passes stops the bill for instances the cafe no longer needs.

questions.takeaway: A regular, expected rush points to predictive scaling, which adds capacity before demand arrives.

read.text: Predictive scaling: Auto Scaling that schedules capacity ahead of anticipated demand.

questions.stem: Every weekday the cafe's order traffic climbs at the same morning hour. The cafe wants instances already running before the rush begins rather than added once it starts. Which Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling approach fits?

options.why: Dynamic scaling reacts once demand changes, so instances would arrive after the rush starts.
Predictive scaling schedules capacity ahead of anticipated demand, so instances are ready in time.
A more powerful single instance is not an Auto Scaling approach for timing capacity.
Scaling in removes instances, which does nothing to prepare for a morning rush.

questions.takeaway: An Auto Scaling group never runs more instances than its maximum capacity, which caps cost.

read.text: Minimum capacity: the floor, launched as soon as the group is created (4 in the example).

questions.stem: The cafe's Auto Scaling group has a minimum capacity of 4, a desired capacity of 6 and a maximum capacity of 12. A holiday promotion drives demand far above normal. Which setting limits how many instances the group can run during the promotion?

options.why: The minimum of 4 is the floor for quiet times, so it limits how few instances run, not how many.
The desired capacity of 6 is the count it aims for at current load, and the group can rise above it.
The group scales out between its minimum and maximum, and the maximum of 12 is the ceiling that caps cost.

options.text: The instance type of its instances
options.why: The instance type sets each instance's CPU and memory, not how many instances the group may run.

questions.takeaway: In an ELB plus Auto Scaling setup, Auto Scaling sets the instance count and ELB only routes traffic.

read.text: They are separate services with complementary jobs: Auto Scaling sets how many instances run, and ELB spreads traffic across them.

questions.stem: The cafe's menu site runs on a fleet of servers behind ELB and gets a rush every Saturday morning. Which service decides how many servers are running during the rush?

options.why: Auto Scaling sets the instance count, adding instances for the rush and removing them afterward.
ELB only spreads traffic across the instances that exist and never adds or removes any.
Compute Optimizer recommends better instance sizes but does not add or remove instances for the rush.
Lambda runs code in response to events and does not manage how many EC2 instances run.

labs.title: Pay less for beans
labs.brief: Pick one way to pay for each of the cafe's four Amazon EC2 workloads so the year costs at most 20,000 lab credits and roast planning at most 100 lab credits, nothing that must keep running is reclaimable, and the loyalty software keeps its per-physical-server license. Hours, months and rates are lab values; a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan bills every hour of its 12-month term, used or not. In this lab both cover only shared hardware, though a real Savings Plan applies whatever the tenancy.

params.label: Till and order server: 730 h a month all year, never pauses
Roast planning: 16 h a month all year, can pause and resume
Holiday promo site: 730 h in one month only, never pauses
Loyalty software: 730 h a month all year, never pauses

goals.label: The year stays within 20,000 lab credits, roast planning within 100 lab credits
goals.hint: A term commitment lowers the rate but bills every hour of the term, so it pays off only for work that runs all the time, and work that can pause and resume can use the deepest discount.

goals.label: Nothing that must keep running sits on capacity AWS may reclaim
goals.hint: AWS can take back its cheapest spare capacity after a short warning, so only a job that can save its progress and resume later belongs there.

goals.label: The loyalty software runs where its physical-server license allows
goals.hint: Ask whether the license needs only hardware kept for the cafe's account, or control over the very physical server the instances are placed on.

lines: A Reserved Instance or a Savings Plan bills every hour of its term, used or not, so it saves only on steady all-year work, and a one-month or part-time job pays less On-Demand.
Spot Instances are the cheapest way to run a job that can save its progress and resume, and the wrong place for one that must not stop.
Only a Dedicated Host gives control over the physical server a physical-server license needs, while a Dedicated Instance isolates hardware but AWS picks the server.

questions.takeaway: Interruptible, non-critical batch work fits Spot Instances and their deep discount on spare capacity.

read.text: Match the model to the usage: unknown means On-Demand, steady means Savings Plans or RIs, and interruptible but never critical means Spot.

questions.stem: Each night the cafe runs a batch job that resizes menu photos. The job can stop at any point and pick up later, and nothing depends on when it finishes. Which pricing option costs the least for this job?

options.why: Dedicated hardware adds isolation the photo job does not need and gives no deep discount.
On-Demand works but charges full price for a job that could run on cheaper spare capacity.
Spot gives the deepest discount, and an interruption only pauses a job that can resume later.
A reservation suits steady, always-on use, not a short nightly job that can be interrupted.

questions.takeaway: When licensing or compliance needs control over the physical server, choose a Dedicated Host.

read.text: A Dedicated Host gives control over instance placement and resource allocation, which helps with compliance and with licensing such as Windows or SQL Server.

questions.stem: The cafe's accounting software uses a SQL Server license tied to the physical server it runs on. The cafe must control which server its instances are placed on. Which option fits?

options.why: Dedicated Instances isolate the hardware, but AWS picks the server, so placement stays out of reach.
Spot capacity can be reclaimed and gives no say over which server the license runs on.
A Dedicated Host is a whole server you control placement on, which suits server-bound licenses.
Default On-Demand instances run on shared hardware that AWS chooses for you.

questions.takeaway: When usage is new or unknown, On-Demand lets you run with no commitment and learn your baseline first.

read.text: On-Demand bills per hour or second, by instance type and OS, and is where most customers learn their baseline usage.

questions.stem: The cafe is trying a new seasonal ordering app and has no idea yet how much compute it will use. It wants to avoid any long-term commitment while it finds out. Which pricing option fits?

options.why: On-Demand asks for no commitment and is how the cafe can learn the app's baseline usage first.
A reservation locks the cafe into a multi-year term before it knows what the app needs.
A Savings Plan commits to an hourly spend for a term, which the cafe cannot size yet.
A whole physical server costs more and answers licensing or compliance needs the app does not have.

labs.title: Queue, topic or event bus
labs.brief: The cafe's new ordering system sends and receives many kinds of message, and each needs to travel differently. Sort each need under the AWS service that carries it best.

cards.text: Drink tickets from the till that wait until a barista is free to make them
Catering requests that the cafe's one busy planner works through, one at a time
Loyalty point updates the rewards app can process later, in the quiet hours
One menu change for the ordering app, the shop signage and the email list, all three having asked for menu news
A text telling a customer their drink is on the counter, sent while they are still waiting
News of offers sent only to customers who signed up for offers, not for new blends or tasting evenings
Notices from the cafe's apps, AWS services and a partner's software, each read on arrival to pick the apps it goes to
Alerts from the bean supplier's software that the stock app reads only in its own format, and only for low stock
Each order placed at the peak, sent to the payment, kitchen and stock services and held for any that is down

goals.label: Work that can wait sits with Amazon SQS
goals.hint: Ask whether the work can sit and wait until the one who handles it is free, then be picked up, done and cleared.

goals.label: Messages pushed to subscribers the moment they are sent sit with Amazon SNS
goals.hint: Ask whether a message must go out the moment it is sent rather than wait to be picked up, perhaps to a person by text or email, and whether subscribers choose what they hear.

goals.label: Events filtered, reshaped or routed onward sit with Amazon EventBridge
goals.hint: Ask whether something in the middle must take in happenings from any sender, work out who cares about each one and adapt it for them before passing it on.

lines: Amazon SQS holds each message until a consumer is ready to take it, so work that can wait never holds up the sender.
Amazon SNS pushes one message to every subscriber of a topic at once, people included, and separate topics let customers choose what they hear.
Amazon EventBridge takes in events from apps, AWS services and partner software, filters and reshapes them, and delivers each to the services that need it, holding it for any that is down.

questions.takeaway: When work arrives faster than a receiver can handle it, or while it is offline, queue it in Amazon SQS.

read.text: It moves any volume of messages between components without losing them, and the receiver need not be available at send time.

questions.stem: The cafe's catering app logs large orders faster than the kitchen planner can review them, and the planner is sometimes offline. Which service lets the orders wait until the planner is ready to work through them?

options.why: SQS keeps each order in a queue until the planner is ready, even when the planner is offline at send time.
SNS pushes messages to subscribers right away and does not keep them for a planner who is offline.
ELB spreads incoming requests across running targets, and it does not hold orders for a planner who is offline.
API Gateway builds and manages APIs, and it does not buffer orders until a busy receiver is free.

questions.takeaway: When people must hear right away by text, email or push, use SNS; SQS is for work that can wait.

read.text: Amazon SNS pushes each message to topic subscribers immediately, including people by push, SMS and email.

questions.stem: The cafe wants to text and email each customer the moment their drink is ready, with nothing held back for later. Which service fits?

options.why: SNS pushes each message to subscribers at once and can reach people by text message and email.
SQS holds messages until a consumer is ready, so it suits deferred work rather than instant alerts to people.
EventBridge routes events between applications and services, and it does not text or email customers directly.
Kinesis Data Streams collects streaming data for processing and does not notify people by text or email.

questions.takeaway: When events from many sources need filtering, transforming and routing to several services, choose EventBridge.

read.text: EventBridge is serverless: custom apps, AWS services or third-party software feed it events, and it forwards them to the applications that need them.

questions.stem: The cafe's app, several AWS services and a third-party payment tool each send a notice whenever something happens, such as a new order. Each notice must be filtered and reshaped, then forwarded to only the services that need it. Which service fits?

options.why: EventBridge takes in notices from custom apps, AWS services and third-party tools, then filters, transforms and delivers them.
SQS holds messages for a consumer to pick up later, but it does not filter, reshape and route them to many services.
SNS pushes each message to its topic subscribers, but it does not reshape the messages from third-party tools first.
Kinesis Data Streams ingests streaming data for apps to read, not filtering, reshaping and routing notices between services.

incidents.title: Lunch rush on the ordering site
incidents.brief: Every weekday lunch, the cafe's ordering site slows down. Some customers wait while one server is swamped and the others barely work, and the manager wants the site steady before next week's promotion.

steps.takeaway: When long sessions pile up unevenly, Least Connections steers each new request to the server holding the fewest.

read.text: Least Connections: routing toward the server with the fewest open connections.

steps.stem: The cafe puts Elastic Load Balancing in front of its ordering servers. Some customers keep a session open far longer than others, so the cafe wants each new request to go to the server holding the smallest number of open sessions right now. Which routing method fits?

options.why: Round Robin cycles through the servers in order, so a server tied up by long sessions still gets its turn.
Least Connections sends each request to the server with the fewest open connections, which is the cafe's goal.
IP Hash pins each customer's IP address to one server, whatever that server's current load is.
Least Response Time picks the fastest-responding server, which need not be the one with the fewest open sessions.

steps.takeaway: An Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity is the floor of instances it always keeps running, whatever the demand.

read.text: Minimum capacity: the floor, launched as soon as the group is created (4 in the example).

steps.stem: The cafe moves its ordering servers into an Auto Scaling group. The manager wants a set number of instances running at all times, even overnight when nobody orders, so the first lunch customers never meet an empty fleet. Which group setting holds that floor?

options.why: Desired capacity is the count the group aims to hold for the current load, so it is a target rather than a floor.
Minimum capacity is the floor, launched as soon as the group exists, so that many instances stay running overnight.
Maximum capacity is the ceiling that caps cost during a surge, so it cannot keep instances running overnight.
Predictive scaling adds capacity ahead of an expected rise, but it sets no lower limit the group never drops below.

steps.takeaway: Auto Scaling sets how many instances run and ELB only spreads traffic across them, so a site needs both.

read.text: ELB never adds, removes or resizes instances itself.

steps.stem: A staff member suggests removing the cafe's Auto Scaling group, since Elastic Load Balancing already sits in front of the ordering servers and can add servers at lunch by itself. Why would that change leave the site short of servers?

options.text: ELB spreads requests but never adds or removes instances
options.why: ELB only routes traffic across the instances that exist, so without Auto Scaling nothing adds servers at lunch.

options.text: ELB grows and shrinks its own capacity as traffic changes
options.why: This is true, but ELB scaling itself only lets it pass more requests, and it still adds no ordering servers.

options.text: ELB is a Regional service that front ends reach by one URL
options.why: This is true, but a single entry point can only route to the servers that exist, so it leaves the count short.

options.text: ELB has its upgrades, patches and failover handled by AWS
options.why: This is true, but AWS running the load balancer's upkeep says nothing about how many ordering servers run at lunch.

incidents.title: The AWS bill that kept creeping up
incidents.brief: The cafe's monthly AWS bill has crept up since spring. The owner asks the IT lead to walk through every workload, from a forgotten test server to the nightly jobs, and trim what can be trimmed without hurting the shop.

steps.takeaway: Stopping an idle instance ends its compute charges and keeps it restartable, while terminating it deletes it.

read.text: Only running instances are billed.

steps.stem: The IT lead finds a test instance that sits unused until a menu trial next month. The lead wants its compute off the bill now without losing the instance before the trial. Which fact about EC2 shows the lead how to do both?

options.text: A stopped instance ends compute charges and can be restarted later
options.why: Only running instances are billed, and a stopped one can be restarted, so stopping it covers both the bill and the trial.

options.text: A terminated instance ends compute charges and is deleted for good
options.why: Terminating does end the charges, but the instance is deleted, so nothing would be left to start for the trial.

options.text: A running instance keeps compute charges going and stays ready to use
options.why: Keeping it running leaves it ready, but it bills for every idle hour, so the server stays on the bill until the trial.

options.text: A smaller size lowers compute charges and can be changed later
options.why: A smaller size still bills for every hour it runs, so the idle month before the trial would still be charged.

steps.takeaway: Right-size by picking the smallest instance size that still performs well, since the size can change later.

read.text: Bigger sizes cost more, so pick the smallest that performs well and switch later if needed.

steps.stem: The cafe's inventory server runs on a large size within its instance family, yet its CPU and memory sit mostly idle all day. How can the IT lead cut its cost while keeping the inventory app working well?

options.text: Move it to a bigger size in the same family
options.why: A bigger size costs more and adds even more of the capacity the server already leaves idle.

options.text: Move it to a smaller size in the same family
options.why: Bigger sizes cost more, so dropping to the smallest size that still performs well cuts the bill, and it can change later.

options.text: Move it to a Dedicated Host of its own
options.why: A Dedicated Host is a whole physical server that costs more than reservations, which raises the bill instead.

options.text: Add more instances of the same size behind ELB
options.why: More instances of the same size multiply the cost of capacity that already sits idle.

steps.takeaway: For steady use that may change instance family or Region, Savings Plans keep the discount where Reserved Instances cannot.

read.text: A Savings Plan applies whatever the Region, tenancy, OS, family or size, while an RI stays within its family and Region.

steps.stem: The cafe's point-of-sale servers run around the clock all year and need dependable capacity and a predictable bill. The IT lead also expects to move them to a newer instance family, and maybe to another Region, during the commitment. Which pricing option keeps its discount through those moves?

options.why: A Reserved Instance discount stays within one instance family and Region, so the planned moves would leave it behind.
A Savings Plan applies whatever the Region, family or size, and it fits critical, always-on use with a predictable bill.
AWS can reclaim Spot capacity, which rules it out for always-on point-of-sale servers that need dependable capacity.
Dedicated Hosts cost more than reservations and serve needs for server control, not a discount that follows moves.

steps.takeaway: Spot Instances are discounted spare capacity that AWS can reclaim after a warning, so jobs on them must be able to stop and resume.

read.text: AWS warns two minutes before reclaiming a Spot Instance, so the job can save progress and resume later.

steps.stem: To save money, the IT lead moves the cafe's nightly sales report job to Spot Instances. One night a warning arrives, and two minutes later the job stops partway through. Which fact about Spot Instances explains the stop?

options.text: AWS can reclaim the spare capacity Spot runs on
options.why: Spot Instances run on spare capacity that AWS can take back after a warning, which is exactly what stopped the job.

options.text: Spot capacity is billed at a discount from On-Demand
options.why: The discount is why the lead chose Spot, but a lower price does not stop a job that is already running.

options.text: A Spot job can save its progress and resume later
options.why: Saving progress is what the job can do with the warning, but it is the response to the stop, not its cause.

options.text: Spot suits batch work and other interruptible jobs
options.why: This says which jobs belong on Spot, which explains the lead's choice, not why the job stopped that night.

incidents.title: Orders vanish when the kitchen app restarts
incidents.brief: On busy mornings, the cafe's ordering app hands each online order straight to the kitchen app. Whenever the kitchen app restarts for an update, a few orders vanish and customers wait for drinks nobody started.

steps.takeaway: Amazon SQS holds messages until a consumer is ready, while Amazon SNS pushes them at once and keeps nothing for later.

read.text: Unlike SQS, SNS does not park messages for later, so in the coffee shop it is the barista calling out a finished drink, not the order board.

steps.stem: The cafe's first fix pushed each online order out to the kitchen app the moment it was sent, so orders that arrived during a restart were still lost. Which service would instead hold each order until the kitchen app is ready to pull it, and let the kitchen app delete it once the drink is made?

options.why: SNS pushes a message to its subscribers at once and does not park it for later, the same loss the first fix had.
API Gateway fronts an API and passes each request on to the backend, so it keeps nothing for a kitchen app that is down.
An SQS queue keeps each message until a consumer pulls it, processes it and deletes it, so orders wait out a restart.
Data Firehose delivers streaming data to lakes, warehouses or analytics tools, not single orders to the kitchen app.

steps.takeaway: A queue between components loosely couples them, so one can fail while the other keeps working.

read.text: Loosely coupled: a message queue sits between them, so A keeps sending while B is down and messages wait until B handles them.

steps.stem: With a queue now between the cafe's ordering app and kitchen app, the kitchen app crashes in the middle of a rush. The ordering app keeps taking orders, and they wait until the kitchen app recovers. Which design property explains this?

options.why: Elasticity grows and shrinks resources as demand changes, which does not explain orders surviving a crash.
Vertical scaling gives an instance more CPU and memory, which says nothing about orders surviving a crash.
Multi-tenancy means instances share a physical host, which does not explain why the ordering app keeps working.
A queue between the apps makes them loosely coupled, so the kitchen app's failure stays contained while orders wait.

steps.takeaway: Amazon EventBridge routes one event to many services and holds it for any service that is down until it recovers.

read.text: EventBridge routes events like "order placed" to each service, copes with peaks, keeps services independent and holds events for a service that is down until it recovers.

steps.stem: The cafe now wants each new order to start a loyalty points update, a stock check and a receipt email, all at once. The loyalty service is sometimes down for updates, and its copy of each order must wait until it recovers. Which service should route each new order to all three of these services?

options.why: SNS can push one message to many subscribers, but it does not park messages, so the loyalty service would miss orders.
EventBridge routes each order to every service that needs it and holds it for a service that is down until it recovers.
In an SQS queue one consumer picks up each message and deletes it, so a single queue does not hand one order to three services.
API Gateway fronts an API and passes each request to one backend, rather than routing one order to several services.

incidents.title: Servers for the new branch
incidents.brief: The cafe is opening a branch across town, and the IT lead has until opening week to stand up the servers behind its ordering kiosks. The lead also wants every later kiosk server to come up the same way as the first.

steps.takeaway: The console suits one-off and visual work, but repeated production launches through it are slow and prone to slips.

read.text: Repeating its screens for every production launch is slow and invites slips like a missed checkbox.

steps.stem: At the main shop, staff built every production server by clicking through the AWS Management Console, and one went live with a setting left unchecked. What does that slip show about the console?

options.text: It fits visual browser work better than typed commands
options.why: The console is a visual browser tool, but being visual does not explain why one server went live with a missed setting.

options.text: It fits checking bills better than writing scripts
options.why: The console is good for bills, but that strength says nothing about the slip in building every production server.

options.text: It fits one-time setups better than repeated launches
options.why: The console suits one-time work, and redoing its screens for every production server is slow and invites a missed setting.

options.text: It fits learning AWS better than calling it from code
options.why: The console is good for learning, but that does not explain why repeating its screens for each server let a setting slip.

steps.takeaway: An EC2 key pair stores the public key on the instance, while you keep the private key to log in.

read.text: Key pair: a public key on the instance and a private key you keep for logging in, created at launch or reused.

steps.stem: While launching the branch's first kiosk server, the IT lead creates a new key pair for logging in. Which part of that key pair is placed on the instance itself?

options.why: The private key stays with the IT lead for logging in, rather than being stored on the instance.
A key pair puts the public key on the instance, and the matching private key is what the lead logs in with.
User data is a launch script that configures the instance, and it is not part of a key pair.
A security group is the instance's firewall, separate from the key pair used to log in.

steps.takeaway: An AMI is a configuration template for launching instances, not a backup of the data they hold.

read.text: It does not set size or networking, and it is no data store or backup, since instance data typically lives on volumes like Amazon EBS.

steps.stem: The IT lead builds a custom AMI from the finished kiosk server. A staff member says the AMI now holds a safe copy of every kiosk order. Which statement should the lead give to correct them?

options.text: One AMI gives every later kiosk server an identical setup
options.why: This is true of an AMI, but it repeats why the lead built one and does not correct the claim about the orders.

options.text: Instance data lives on Amazon EBS volumes, not in the AMI
options.why: An AMI holds the OS, software and setup for launches and is no data store or backup, so the orders need their own backup.

options.text: The instance type, not the AMI, sets each server's hardware
options.why: This is true, since the instance type sets the hardware, but it says nothing about where the kiosk orders are kept.

options.text: AMIs can also come from AWS or AWS Marketplace vendors
options.why: This is true, since AMIs come from AWS and AWS Marketplace too, but where an AMI comes from does not touch the claim about the orders.
